about: The resume verdict's rubric: what a hiring manager checks in a first read. The resume reader (server/intake.py) scores each 1 to 5 against these anchors and the check page (check/check.js) shows the labels. Change it here and nowhere else; bump version when an anchor changes, since stored scores were made against the old one.

anchors.1: No target visible: the title and summary point somewhere else, or nowhere.
anchors.3: The target can be guessed from the history, but the top doesn't say it.
anchors.5: The first lines name the role and level, and everything below supports it.

anchors.1: Duties only: what they were responsible for, never what changed.
anchors.3: Some results, few numbers a reader can hold onto.
anchors.5: Most bullets state a result, many with a number.

anchors.3: A link or two, but hard to judge or unrelated to the target.
anchors.5: Links to shipped, relevant work, near the top.

anchors.1: Ownership and scale well below the level they want.
anchors.3: Mixed: some work at the level, much below it.
anchors.5: Ownership and scale match or exceed the level they want.

anchors.1: Dense walls of text; the key facts are buried.
anchors.3: Readable, but the point takes a while to find.
anchors.5: The role, the strongest result and the stack are visible at a glance.

anchors.1: Little overlap with what the target role usually asks for.
anchors.3: Partial overlap, or the overlap isn't stated clearly.
anchors.5: Strong overlap, stated where a reader sees it.

peers.note: A percentile shows only when at least this many resumes for the same role have been read and saved; until then the page says how many there are.
